A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same scaling-law research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model training experiments, loss-curve predictions, warmup and annealing analyses, and synthetic scaling-law fitting results.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds MoE experiments, longer-horizon and held-out-model predictions, and original fitting analyses of public training curves.

M1.justification: The proposed forward-area and annealing-momentum formulation, model-size extension, and Huber-loss fitting procedure remain unchanged. MoE is an additional experimental architecture, not a new component of the proposed scaling-law method.

E1.justification: Appendix C.4 adds externally generated BLOOM and OLMo training trajectories, including OLMo's Pile evaluation losses. The existing Fineweb, RedPajama-CC and multilingual-mixture coverage remains. New model architectures and longer training budgets primarily change experimental settings, not the underlying language-modeling task.

E2.justification: Chinchilla remains the explicit alternative scaling-law comparator, and the alternative annealing-term formulations in Section 6.3 are retained. BLOOM and OLMo supply additional curves to fit; they are not competing prediction methods.

E3.justification: The main model-size experiment changes from fitting all five sizes to fitting four and predicting the held-out 1214.4M model (v1 Figure 6b; v2 Figure 7b). Added protocols include 60K-step MoE fitting with WSD curves and fitting 30K-step curves to predict a 350K-step, 1.7B-model run (Appendices C.2–C.3). These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial generalization checks addressing transfer to MoE architectures, extrapolation beyond ten times the fitting horizon, and prediction at a held-out model size. Existing warmup, optimizer-momentum, decay-factor, annealing-function and alternative-formulation analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same means and standard deviations of R-squared over 1,000 sampled parameter tuples in Table 1. v2 introduces no new seed counts, repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: New results include MoE prediction errors of 0.191%, 0.134% and 0.273% (Figure 24), a 350K-step prediction error of 0.359% (Figure 26), and BLOOM/OLMo fitting R-squared values of 0.99640/0.99869 (Figure 27). The main model-size fit changes from R-squared 0.99889 to 0.99880 under the revised holdout protocol, so these values are not a same-setting performance comparison.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly supplies the initial condition m1 = 0 in Section 3.2 and corrects the undefined k index in the alternative momentum recurrence to i (v1 Equation 10; v2 Equation 9). These are limited mathematical-specification corrections; the central derivation, model-size extension and Chinchilla-reduction argument remain.

C1.justification: The full-trajectory scaling law, unseen-scheduler prediction, model-size extension and computational-saving claims remain. v2 adds explicit contribution claims about validity across model architectures and fitting publicly released model curves in the abstract and introduction, modestly extending the stated contribution set.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 adds a loss-surface interpretation in which annealing reduces oscillation along a slide's walls. Section 6.1 additionally qualifies the connection between momentum-window size and optimal annealing duration by requiring smoothly changing learning rates. Existing limitations concerning near-zero learning rates, unexplained delay mechanisms and post-training applicability remain.

D1.justification: Table 3 documents new MoE and long-run configurations, including expert selection, auxiliary-loss weight and sequence lengths, and newly discloses sequence length for retained settings. v2 also supplies implementation-code access information and identifies the public-log sources and exact evaluation fields used in Figure 27. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the retained experiments.

R1.justification: v2 broadens citations covering scaling-law variants, MoE and public models, and attributes the existing cyclic scheduler to Smith (2017). Its central positioning relative to Chinchilla and its disagreement with Hägele et al. remain. The renamed Llama references correspond to works already cited in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries, derivation and takeaway sections undergo extensive rewriting and streamlining. WSD background moves into Appendix D, supplementary experiments are organized into Appendix C subsections, and a future-applications subsection is added. This is a broad narrative and structural revision beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds the loss-surface illustration in Figure 6 and experimental displays in Figures 23–27, expands Table 3 into two configuration blocks, and revises numerous axes, legends and captions. Retained appendix fitting and prediction figures are consolidated and rearranged; the older model-size and annealing-function plots remain under new numbering.

improvement.justification: v1 fitted all sizes in its main model-size example; v2 holds out the largest size and adds MoE and 30K-to-350K-step prediction tests. These address important gaps in evidence for generalization. Public-model fits, expanded settings and code-access information further strengthen validation and reproducibility. Some new annotations are inconsistent, such as the exponent sign in Figure 23, but these limited defects do not outweigh the substantive validation gains.
